rows.selection_reason: 1) Evidence/uncertainty: No experiments have been completed, so there is zero information about which modality, encoder, profile setting, or aggregation strategy is most important. The entire design space is unexplored. 2) What this tests: config_001 is the simplest possible configuration—RNA-only, single-profile, PCA (n=2000) with no aggregation or fusion. It establishes a minimal performance floor and tells us whether the basic linear structure in the RNA data is already informative for the task. 3) Why it is the best first experiment: Starting with the simplest, fastest, and most interpretable baseline is the most information-efficient use of the first budget slot. It gives a clear reference point against which every subsequent configuration (learned encoders, multiprofile aggregation, image modality, multimodal fusion) can be compared. If PCA-single-profile already performs well, we know the task is relatively easy and can focus budget on marginal gains; if it performs poorly, we know we must invest in richer representations. Choosing a more complex first experiment (e.g., scGPT or multimodal) would confound multiple design choices at once and make it harder to attribute performance to specific decisions. A cheap, simple baseline maximizes the information gained per experiment.

With only one completed experiment (config_001: rna_only/singleprofile/pca_n2000 at ~48.5% accuracy), evidence is extremely sparse. The most critical uncertainty is whether the image modality carries discriminative signal at all, which determines the entire direction of the search (RNA-focused vs. image-focused vs. multimodal). config_010 (image_only, singleprofile, resnet50) is the cleanest single-variable comparison to config_001: it changes only the modality while keeping the profile setting (singleprofile) and architecture simplicity (no aggregation, no fusion) identical. If image-only substantially outperforms RNA-only, we should prioritize image encoders and multimodal fusion; if it underperforms, RNA is the dominant signal and we should focus on RNA encoder and profile choices. This experiment maximally reduces uncertainty about the most consequential design axis before committing budget to more complex multimodal or multiprofile configurations.

Evidence: RNA (pca_n2000, singleprofile) achieves 48.5% acc / 46.4% F1, while image (resnet50, singleprofile) is very weak at 20.8% acc. RNA is clearly the dominant modality, so improving its representation is the highest-priority question. Uncertainty: We do not yet know whether a learned, domain-specific encoder (scvi_n200) can outperform a simple linear PCA projection, or whether PCA already captures the relevant signal. This experiment (config_004) is a clean single-variable change from config_001—only the RNA encoder changes (pca_n2000 → scvi_n200), keeping singleprofile and no aggregation/fusion—so any performance difference can be attributed to the representation choice. If scvi substantially beats PCA, it justifies investing further in learned encoders and multimodal fusion with a stronger RNA backbone; if it does not, it tells us PCA is sufficient and we should redirect budget toward profile settings, image encoders, or fusion strategies. Under the limited budget, isolating the representation effect on our strongest modality is the most informative next step before committing to more complex multimodal or multiprofile configurations.

Evidence: RNA-only models (0.485–0.520) far outperform image-only (0.208), establishing RNA as the dominant modality. Within RNA singleprofile, scvi_n200 (0.520) beats pca_n2000 (0.485), suggesting a learned latent representation is preferable. Uncertainty: It is unclear whether multiprofile aggregation adds value over singleprofile, which is a fundamental architectural decision that gates an entire branch of the search space. Question tested: config_005 (rna_only, multiprofile, scvi_n200, avgpool) is a near-minimal change from config_004 (same encoder, singleprofile), isolating the effect of multiprofile + simple average-pool aggregation. Why best next: It directly compares against the current best (config_004) with only one design axis changed, giving a clean read on whether multiprofile is worth the added complexity. If multiprofile helps, the next step is to test transformer aggregation (config_006); if it does not, we can prune the multiprofile branch and focus budget on encoder or fusion questions. This maximizes information per experiment under the limited budget.

Evidence: config_005 (scVI_n200, multiprofile, avgpool) achieved 0.650 accuracy, a large jump over config_004 (scVI_n200, singleprofile) at 0.520, confirming that multi-profile with aggregation is highly beneficial. However, we only have one data point on aggregation (avgpool). Uncertainty: it is unknown whether a more expressive aggregation (transformer) further improves over simple average pooling, or whether avgpool already captures most of the multi-profile benefit. This experiment (config_006: scVI_n200, multiprofile, transformer) is a clean single-variable comparison against config_005—only the aggregation changes. It directly isolates the effect of aggregation method while holding encoder and profile setting fixed. Under a limited budget, resolving whether transformer aggregation adds value over avgpool is critical because the answer propagates to every future multimodal or multiprofile experiment, making this the highest-information next step.

Evidence: Multiprofile + scvi_n200 is the clear winner so far (config_005/006 at ~0.65), and the multiprofile effect is large (~0.13 gain over singleprofile). Aggregation (avgpool vs transformer) makes negligible difference. The image modality appears weak (resnet50 image-only at 0.208). Uncertainty: We have not tested whether scgpt, a more specialized RNA foundation-model encoder, can outperform scvi_n200 in the multiprofile setting. Question: config_008 (scgpt, multiprofile, avgpool) directly compares against config_005 (scvi_n200, multiprofile, avgpool) by changing only the RNA encoder, cleanly isolating the encoder effect. Why best next: This is a single-variable, high-information experiment in the most promising region. If scgpt improves, we gain a new best and a direction to extend into multimodal; if it matches or lags, we confirm scvi_n200 is near-optimal and can redirect budget toward testing whether a better image encoder (ViT-L) or multimodal fusion adds value on top of the RNA signal. It avoids the risk of spending a run on a multimodal config that adds complexity while the RNA encoder question remains open.

Evidence: RNA-only multiprofile with scvi_n200 is the clear current best (0.653 acc, config_006), with aggregation choice (avgpool vs transformer) making negligible difference. Image-only with resnet50 is very weak (0.208), raising the question of whether image features can add complementary signal when fused with the strong RNA representation. The biggest open uncertainty is whether multimodal fusion can push beyond the 0.653 RNA-only ceiling. This experiment tests that directly: it pairs the best-validated RNA configuration (scvi_n200, multiprofile, transformer) with the already-characterized resnet50 image encoder and uses simple concat fusion. By holding the image encoder to resnet50 (the only one we've seen), we isolate the fusion question without confounding with an untested image backbone. If multimodal helps, the next step is to try ViT-L; if it does not, we learn that image features (at least at this quality level) are not complementary to the RNA signal, redirecting effort toward RNA-side improvements. This is the highest-information next experiment under the limited budget.

Evidence: config_032 (multimodal, multiprofile, scvi_n200, resnet50, transformer, concat) is the current best at 0.688 acc, outperforming the best RNA-only config_006 (0.653) by ~3.5 points, confirming the image modality adds value. However, we have only tested concat fusion; weighted fusion remains entirely untested. Question: Does weighted fusion outperform concat in the multimodal setting, or is concat already near-optimal? This experiment changes exactly one variable (fusion: concat→weighted) relative to config_032, giving a clean A/B comparison that isolates the fusion method effect. Why this is the best next step: Under a limited budget, testing the fusion strategy at the current best configuration is the most efficient way to either (a) find a free improvement that lifts the ceiling for all future multimodal experiments, or (b) confirm concat is sufficient and redirect effort toward other levers (image encoder, aggregation). It avoids the risk of changing multiple variables simultaneously and directly reduces uncertainty about a core architectural choice before scaling to more complex configurations.

Evidence: The current best is config_033 (scVI + ResNet50 + multiprofile + transformer + weighted) at 0.713 acc. The image modality is very weak alone (ResNet50 single: 0.208) yet adds ~6 points in the multimodal setting, suggesting it carries complementary signal. Key uncertainty: is the image encoder quality (ResNet50) the bottleneck limiting how much the image contributes, or is the signal inherently limited? Question: config_039 is identical to config_033 except the image encoder is swapped from ResNet50 to ImageNet-pretrained ViT-L, isolating the effect of image representation quality. Why best next: It is a clean single-variable extension of the best-performing configuration, directly testing whether a stronger image encoder unlocks more multimodal gain. If ViT-L substantially improves over ResNet50, it confirms the image modality has untapped signal and justifies further image-encoder investment; if not, it tells us the image contribution is near its ceiling and effort should shift to RNA-side improvements or fusion strategy. This is more informative than testing aggregation (avgpool vs transformer showed negligible difference in RNA-only) or fusion (weighted already beats concat by ~2.5 pts).

Evidence: The current best is config_039 (scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l + transformer + weighted, acc 0.725). We have strong evidence that weighted fusion outperforms concat in multimodal (config_033: 0.713 vs config_032: 0.688 with resnet50, a ~2.5% gap). However, we have not tested whether this fusion advantage holds with the VIT image encoder, which produces a different representation geometry. Question: config_038 (identical to config_039 except fusion=concat) isolates the single variable of fusion type under the best-performing image encoder. Why this is the best next experiment: It is a clean one-variable comparison with the current best, directly testing whether the weighted-fusion advantage generalizes across image encoders. If concat approaches weighted with VIT, it suggests the VIT representation is more naturally aligned and a simpler fusion suffices (practical simplification). If the gap persists or widens, it confirms weighted fusion is a robust, encoder-independent design choice and we can confidently exploit it in all future multimodal configurations. Under a limited budget, this single experiment reduces uncertainty about a key architectural decision without changing multiple factors simultaneously.
